newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN drops role in sanctions meet after US rails.
newsitem.headline: UN drops role in sanctions meet after US rails.

text.p: The United Nations said on Friday it had dropped plans -- after intervention by the United States -- to provide a site for a forum next month on economic sanctions to be attended by senior Libyan and Iraqi officials.

U.N. spokeswoman Therese Gastaut told a news briefing the gathering, organised by a private Swiss foundation and to have taken place at the world body's European headquarters, the Palais des Nations, would now be held at a Geneva hotel.
"It was felt that as the programme developed holding it on U.N. premises could cause confusion and that it would be seen as a United Nations meeting, which it is not," Gastaut said.

Libya's Foreign Minister Omar Mountacer and Iran's Ali Akbar Velayati had already accepted invitations to speak at the meeting, organisers said earlier this week, and a high-level team from Baghdad was also expected.

Jean-Paul Carteron, founder of the Swiss-based "Universal Forum", told a news conference on Wednesday that he had also invited Cuba's President Fidel Castro, expected to be in Rome at the time attending a U.N. conference on food supplies.

Gastaut said several diplomatic missions had contacted the U.N. Geneva office, whose Director-General Vladimir Petrovsky is currently in New York, over the gathering. The U.S. mission had sent a formal letter.

"We represent the members of the United Nations and we obviously respect their views," she said. "We also realised when we saw the full programme that the Palais des Nations was not the right place for the meeting."

A U.S. spokesman confirmed that Ambassador Daniel Spiegel had written to Petrovsky. "We pointed out that in view of the way the programme was turning out, the United Nations did not seem the appropriate place to hold the meeting," he said.

The official topic of the gathering, to which Carteron said he had also invited the United States to send speakers as well as other countries and top U.N. officials from New York, was "Sanctions: Rationale and Impact."

The Swiss lawyer, who runs an annual forum for international business and political leaders in the Swiss mountain resort of Crans-Montana, said the agenda was to discuss freely how far sanctions had the effect intended on targetted countries.

Billed speakers at the session, which is also due to discuss the long-standing unilateral U.S. economic embargo on Cuba and the recent Helms-Burton law aimed at foreign investment on the island, are mainly academics.

But they also include the New York Director of the U.N. Sanctions Committee Joseph Stephanides, who supervises implementation of sanctions against Iraq and Libya and the former Yugoslavia, and Bosnia's U.N. envoy Mohammed Sacirbey.

U.N. officials said Carteron's organisation, which itself had no immediate comment on the decision, had agreed to the change of venue. His foundation had been due to pay the world body for use of the premises, they added.

The U.S. mission did not release the text of the letter from Spiegel, a vocal supporter of the United Nations but who also backs Washington's demand that Secretary-General Boutros Boutros-Ghali stand down at the end of this year.

But U.S. officials indicated they saw no reason why the U.N. should provide a platform for a private gathering at which representatives of what they called "rogue states" could attack sanctions policies.
